summary: This memo discusses subnets, parts of one Internet network that are logically visible as separate pieces, and proposes procedures for using them, including how to handle routing. Organizations used subnets instead of getting many separate network numbers.

plainLanguage.summary: This proposal explains how one Internet network number can cover several local networks. It divides the local part of an address so hosts and gateways can distinguish the subnets.

questions: why use subnets instead of more network numbers
subtitle: A proposal to divide one Internet network number into subnets for separate local networks.

tldr.problem: An organization with multiple local cables could request a separate Internet network number for each or hide the cables behind bridges.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal divides the local part of an Internet address into a subnet field and a host field, and describes masks, broadcasts, and a way to discover the field width.
tldr.outcome: RFC 917 proposes procedures for discussion and describes a way to support multiple local networks under one network number.

facts.label: Subnet mask example
facts.value: 255.255.0.0 for Class A with an eight-bit subnet field

today: RFC 917 is a proposal from October 1984 that requests discussion and suggestions for improvement. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why an Organization Might Need Subnets
sections.content:
The original Internet address model identified a network and then a host. Larger organizations sometimes needed several local cables because of different technologies, cable limits, congestion, or distance between buildings.

Giving every cable a separate Internet network number would spread local details into routing tables. Transparent bridges did not work for every LAN technology. RFC 917 proposes explicit subnets under one network number, requiring modest changes to IP implementations on subnetted networks.
sections.plainLanguage: An organization may need several local networks but still want one Internet network number. Subnetting adds a local subnet identifier instead of advertising each cable separately.

sections.title: Network, Subnet, and Host Fields
sections.content:
The proposal reads an Internet address as a network number, a subnet number, and a host number. The subnet field is the most significant part of the local address, and its width is fixed for a given network. A zero-width subnet field means that the network is not subnetted.

The host field must be at least one bit wide. The proposal selects a variable-width subnet field so each network can choose how its local address bits are divided. It rejects recursively dividing the host field into additional subnet levels.
sections.plainLanguage: A subnetted address has a network part, a subnet part, and a host part. Each network chooses one subnet-field width and uses it consistently.

sections.title: Masks and Broadcast Addresses
sections.content:
A host stores a 32-bit mask with bits set for the network and subnet fields. It applies the mask to its own address and the destination address to decide whether the destination is local or requires a gateway. A Class A network with an eight-bit subnet field uses the example mask 255.255.0.0.

The proposal distinguishes a broadcast to the physical network, a specific network, and a specific subnet. The all-ones address 255.255.255.255 is limited to the local physical network and must not be forwarded by a gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: A host uses a mask to decide whether a destination is on its subnet. Broadcast addresses can target the physical network, a whole network, or one subnet.

sections.title: Learning the Subnet-Field Width
sections.content:
A host can learn the subnet-field width from stored configuration or by asking on the local network. For diskless hosts, the proposal defines ICMP Address Format Request and Address Format Reply messages. A host broadcasts a request, and a gateway or another host acting for it replies with the width in the Code field.

If no reply arrives, the host assumes a width of zero. A gateway should send a reply based on the configured width, not a guess. The protocol is optional; a host with stored information can use it instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A host can ask a gateway how many address bits identify a subnet. If no answer arrives, the proposal says to assume subnets are not in use.

sections.title: Routing and Unmodified Hosts
sections.content:
With subnets, a host must determine whether a destination is on the same physical network before choosing direct delivery or a gateway. A default gateway and ICMP Host Redirects can hide some routing choices from hosts, but gateways and multihomed hosts need routing information.

The memo describes an ARP-based method for certain unmodified hosts on broadcast LANs. A subnet gateway can answer an ARP request with its own hardware address and then forward the packet. The memo notes that this method cannot preserve a connection if that gateway fails.
sections.plainLanguage: A host needs to know whether the destination is local or must go through a gateway. In some networks, a gateway can answer ARP for a destination and forward packets for an unmodified host.
